result: T. gondii is an obligate intracellular parasite that infects warm-blooded animals and humans through ingestion of tissue cysts or oocysts. Following oral ingestion, the parasite disseminates as tachyzoites and differentiates to bradyzoites within cysts in response to immune pressure, establishing chronic infections in muscle and brain tissues.
evaluation: Claims C1-C4 provide well-established background information about T. gondii biology, transmission routes, and life cycle stages. All claims are supported by appropriate citations to prior literature (Dubey 2010, Jones and Dubey 2012, Drewry and Sibley 2019, Watts et al. 2015, Jeffers et al. 2018, Mayoral et al. 2020), representing accepted knowledge in the field.

result: The tachyzoite lytic cycle is controlled by intracellular Ca2+ signaling. Artificially elevating Ca2+ triggers microneme secretion needed for motility and invasion, with cytosolic Ca2+ from internal stores being both sufficient and necessary for these processes. Ca2+ increases also drive PLP1 secretion to facilitate PVM rupture and egress.
evaluation: Claims C5-C10 describe established mechanisms of Ca2+ signaling in tachyzoites, all supported by appropriate citations to prior work (Lourido and Moreno 2015, Carruthers and Sibley 1999, Lovett et al. 2002, Vieira and Moreno 2000, Pace et al. 2014, Kafsack et al. 2009). This provides essential background for the comparative studies with bradyzoites.

result: Ca2+ signaling in tachyzoites is initiated by cGMP-generating guanylate cyclase that activates PKG, which stimulates PI-PLC to produce IP3 and release intracellular Ca2+. Ca2+ then activates downstream effectors including CDPKs, C2 domain proteins, and calmodulin orthologues required for invasion and egress. PKAc1 subsequently dampens Ca2+ signaling after invasion.
evaluation: Claims C11-C20 describe the established Ca2+ signaling cascade in tachyzoites, with all claims supported by appropriate citations to prior literature (Brown and Sibley 2018, Bisio et al. 2019, Yang et al. 2019, Brown et al. 2017, Lovett et al. 2002, Fang et al. 2006, Bullen et al. 2016, Balestra et al. 2021, Lourido and Moreno 2015, Lourido et al. 2012, McCoy et al. 2012, Tagoe et al. 2021, Long et al. 2017, Jia et al. 2017, Uboldi et al. 2018, Brown et al. 2019). This provides comprehensive background on tachyzoite Ca2+ regulation.

result: T. gondii controls intracellular Ca2+ through Ca2+ channels, transporters, and pumps at the plasma membrane and intracellular stores. The ER serves as a major Ca2+ storage site with SERCA-type Ca2+ ATPase mediating uptake (inhibited by thapsigargin), while TgA1 transports Ca2+ to acidocalcisomes. Both intracellular and extracellular parasites can take up Ca2+ from their environment.
evaluation: Claims C21-C30 describe established mechanisms of Ca2+ homeostasis in T. gondii, all supported by appropriate citations (Lourido and Moreno 2015, Hortua Triana et al. 2018, Nagamune and Sibley 2006, Prole et al. 2011, Thastrup et al. 1990, Nagamune et al. 2007, Moreno and Zhong 1996, Luo et al. 2004, Pace et al. 2014, Vella et al. 2021). This provides essential background on Ca2+ regulation mechanisms.

result: Various Ca2+ indicators have been used to monitor Ca2+ levels in T. gondii, including chemical dyes like Fluo-4/AM for extracellular parasites and genetically encoded indicators (GCaMP5, GCaMP6f, GCaMP7) for visualizing dynamic Ca2+ signals in both intracellular and extracellular tachyzoites.
evaluation: Claims C31-C32 describe established Ca2+ imaging methodologies, supported by appropriate citations (Nagamune et al. 2007, Lovett and Sibley 2003, Vella et al. 2021, Sidik et al. 2016, Borges-Pereira et al. 2015, Brown et al. 2016). This provides methodological context for the current study's approach.

result: Little is known about Ca2+ signaling in bradyzoites, which divide asynchronously and undergo periodic cyst rupture to maintain chronic infection. Bradyzoites can be studied in vitro through alkaline pH stress induction or spontaneous development in certain cell lines. While stage conversion has been extensively studied, signaling pathways controlling the bradyzoite lytic cycle remain poorly characterized.
evaluation: Claims C33-C42 establish the knowledge gap and provide background on bradyzoite biology. Claims are supported by appropriate citations (Watts et al. 2015, Ferguson et al. 1989, Frenkel and Escajadillo 1987, Hofflin et al. 1987, Soete et al. 1993, Swierzy and Lüder 2015, Halonen et al. 1996, Jeffers et al. 2018, White et al. 2014). This effectively motivates the current study.

result: The study demonstrates that bradyzoites exhibit dampened Ca2+ levels, reduced microneme secretion, and minimal egress in response to Ca2+ agonists. Ratiometric Ca2+ imaging revealed lower basal Ca2+ and reduced stored Ca2+ in ER and acidocalcisomes, associated with reduced expression of Ca2+ ATPases. Incubation with Ca2+ plus glucose leads to rapid recovery of Ca2+, ATP levels, and motility in extracellular bradyzoites.
evaluation: Claims C43-C48 summarize the main findings of the study, which are supported by extensive experimental data presented in Figures 1-8. The claims are internally consistent and represent the core conclusions drawn from multiple complementary experimental approaches including Ca2+ imaging, microneme secretion assays, egress assays, ratiometric measurements, gene expression analysis, and metabolic recovery experiments.

result: Bradyzoites show significantly impaired egress compared to tachyzoites in response to Ca2+ ionophore A23187 or zaprinast. A23187 induced complete egress of tachyzoites from disrupted PVs while only a few bradyzoites were released from largely intact cysts. Bradyzoites also migrated shorter distances and moved more slowly than tachyzoites after induced egress.
evaluation: Claims C49-C53 are directly supported by data in Figure 1A-D showing quantitative differences in egress rates, migration distances, and speeds between tachyzoites and bradyzoites. Statistical analyses (Mann-Whitney tests, p<0.001) confirm significant differences. The experimental design includes appropriate controls and replicates (n=20).

result: MIC2-Gluc reporter is expressed and localized to the apical pole in both tachyzoites and bradyzoites, though MIC2-GLuc and M2AP are expressed at lower levels in bradyzoites. MIC2 and M2AP co-localize to the apical region in bradyzoites. Bradyzoites secreted significantly less MIC2-Gluc protein compared to tachyzoites in response to Ca2+ agonists zaprinast and ionomycin.
evaluation: Claims C54-C57 are supported by IFA data (Figure 2B, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A), western blotting (Figure 2C), and Gaussia luciferase assays (Figure 2D). The data demonstrate both the presence and localization of the reporter and quantitative differences in secretion between stages. FACS sorting was used to enrich reporter-expressing parasites, strengthening the quantitative secretion measurements.

result: Using the FNR-mCherry secretion reporter, A23187 stimulated fast leakage from the PV surrounding tachyzoites but FNR-mCherry was not released from bradyzoite cysts after A23187 stimulation. Trypsin digestion of the cyst wall caused rapid dissipation of FNR-mCherry, confirming it was present in the cyst matrix. These findings demonstrate dampened microneme secretion by bradyzoites.
evaluation: Claims C58-C61 are supported by time-lapse microscopy data (Figure 2F, Figure 2G, Figure 2—videos 1-3). The trypsin control (C60) is critical for validating that FNR-mCherry was indeed secreted into the cyst matrix and not simply absent or trapped. The conclusion (C61) is a reasonable inference from the combined data showing reduced secretion by multiple independent methods.

result: Using the BAG1-mCherry GCaMP6f dual reporter, ionophore treatment induced rapid, high-level Ca2+ increases in tachyzoites but delayed, weaker responses in bradyzoites. The time to reach peak Ca2+ increased with bradyzoite development time (4-7 days). Both A23187 and zaprinast elicited slower Ca2+ increases and lower fold changes in bradyzoites. Motile bradyzoites showed higher, oscillating GCaMP6f signals but reduced overall motility compared to tachyzoites.
evaluation: Claims C62-C69 are supported by extensive time-lapse microscopy data (Figure 3B-G, Figure 3—videos 1-2). The dual reporter system allows simultaneous monitoring of stage (BAG1-mCherry) and Ca2+ (GCaMP6f). Control experiments (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C-D) ruled out expression differences as the cause of reduced responses. Statistical analyses confirm significant differences (n=10, p<0.001). The ~70% mature bradyzoite population at 7 days (C70, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A-B) validates the differentiation protocol.

result: Approximately 70% of parasites were mature bradyzoites (BAG1-positive, SAG1-negative) in cysts induced for 7 days at pH 8.2.
evaluation: Claim C70 is supported by quantitative IFA data using spinning disc confocal microscopy (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A-B). The criterion of BAG1+/SAG1- for mature bradyzoites is appropriate. Statistical analysis shows significant increase in mature bradyzoites from 3 to 7 days (Kruskal-Wallis test with Dunn's correction, p<0.001, n=20). This validates the 7-day time point used throughout the study.

result: Bradyzoites formed spontaneously in differentiated C2C12 muscle myocytes showed much lower rate and amplitude of GCaMP6f signal increases compared to tachyzoites in myoblasts, with delayed time to peak Ca2+ and significantly lower motility in response to A23187 and zaprinast. These findings confirm dampened Ca2+ dynamics in naturally formed bradyzoites.
evaluation: Claims C71-C73, C76 are supported by data from the C2C12 myocyte differentiation system (Figure 4A-E). This system provides an important control showing that dampened Ca2+ responses are not simply artifacts of alkaline pH stress induction. Myocyte differentiation was confirmed by skeletal myosin staining (Figure 4A). Quantitative analyses show significant differences (Student's t-test, p<0.001, n=10).

result: Bradyzoites within ex vivo cysts isolated from chronically infected mouse brains demonstrated lower and slower GCaMP6f fluorescence changes compared to extracellular tachyzoites in response to Ca2+ agonists. Strikingly, no egressed bradyzoites were observed from ex vivo cysts treated with A23187 and zaprinast, although all bradyzoites within cysts became motile after stimulation.
evaluation: Claims C74-C75 are supported by ex vivo experiments using cysts harvested from chronically infected mice at 30 days post-infection (Figure 4F-H, Figure 4—videos 1-2). This provides critical validation that dampened Ca2+ responses occur in authentic tissue cysts, not just in vitro models. The observation that bradyzoites become motile but do not egress (C75) suggests the cyst wall creates a physical barrier, which is further explored in later experiments.

result: Extracellular bradyzoites liberated from cysts by trypsin showed slower increases in GCaMP6f fluorescence and slower Ca2+ responses to A23187 and zaprinast compared to tachyzoites. SYTOX staining confirmed that extracellular bradyzoites remained viable after trypsin treatment.
evaluation: Claims C77-C79 are supported by time-lapse microscopy of extracellular parasites (Figure 5A-C, Figure 5—videos 1-2). The viability control using SYTOX staining (C79, Figure 5C) is essential for validating that reduced Ca2+ responses are not due to cell death from trypsin treatment. This demonstrates that dampened Ca2+ responses are intrinsic to bradyzoites, not artifacts of the cyst environment.

result: Extracellular bradyzoites showed delayed and lower amplitude Ca2+ responses to ionomycin and thapsigargin (ER Ca2+ release) compared to tachyzoites, indicative of lower ER-stored Ca2+. Bradyzoites treated with NH4Cl showed no meaningful GCaMP6f fluorescence change, suggesting lack of mobilizable acidic Ca2+. Similar dampened responses were observed using Fluo-8 AM, confirming bradyzoites are less able to mobilize Ca2+ from ER and acidic stores.
evaluation: Claims C80-C83 are supported by experiments using specific agonists to probe different Ca2+ stores (Figure 5D-E). Ionomycin and thapsigargin target ER Ca2+, while NH4Cl releases acidic store Ca2+. The use of both GCaMP6f (C80-C81) and Fluo-8 AM (C82) provides independent validation and rules out reporter-specific artifacts. The conclusion (C83) is well-supported by the combined data from multiple agonists and reporters.

result: Using a ratiometric GCaMP6f/mTagBFP2 reporter, significant reductions in fluorescence intensity ratios were observed in both intracellular and extracellular bradyzoites relative to tachyzoites, indicative of lower resting Ca2+ levels. Changes in GCaMP6f fluorescence were much slower and of lower amplitude in bradyzoites in response to Ca2+ agonists. Lower resting and peak Ca2+ levels in extracellular bradyzoites indicate reduced activity or expression of Ca2+ influx mechanisms.
evaluation: Claims C84-C86 are supported by ratiometric imaging data (Figure 6A-F). The ratiometric approach using Ca2+-insensitive mTagBFP2 as an internal control is methodologically sound and addresses potential concerns about differential reporter expression. The CRISPR/Cas9-mediated targeted insertion (Figure 6A, Figure 6—figure supplement 1) ensures proper expression. Western blotting confirms equal expression of both reporters (Figure 6C). Statistical analyses show significant differences (Student's t-test, p<0.001, n=10).

result: RT-PCR analysis revealed significant reduction in relative expression levels of Ca2+-related genes in bradyzoites compared to tachyzoites, including TgSERCA, TgA1, TgPMCA1, TgA2, Ca2+/H+ exchanger, and TgTRPPL-2. These findings indicate that bradyzoites have lower levels of stored Ca2+, which is associated with overall downregulation of Ca2+-related pumps and channels.
evaluation: Claims C87-C88 are supported by quantitative RT-PCR data (Figure 6G) showing significant reductions in expression of multiple Ca2+ transporters and channels (multiple Student's t-tests, p<0.01 or p<0.001). The analysis included appropriate housekeeping gene controls (actin) and stage-specific markers (SAG1, BAG1). The data come from two independent experiments with triplicate samples. The conclusion (C88) reasonably links reduced gene expression to the observed phenotypes of lower Ca2+ stores and responses.

result: Trypsin treatment and release of bradyzoites from cysts did not result in immediate changes in Ca2+ levels or motility during 5-10 min monitoring. The majority of bradyzoites failed to show enhanced GCaMP fluorescence or initiate gliding motility after release. However, a small subset of bradyzoites that did undergo gliding displayed patterns reminiscent of tachyzoite motility including circular gliding, with fluctuations in GCaMP6f fluorescence similar to oscillating Ca2+ patterns previously described in gliding tachyzoites.
evaluation: Claims C89-C92 are supported by time-lapse microscopy data (Figure 7A-D, Figure 7—videos 1-2). The observation that cyst wall degradation does not immediately trigger Ca2+ changes or motility (C89-C90) is important for understanding bradyzoite biology. The subset showing motility with Ca2+ oscillations (C91-C92) demonstrates that the Ca2+ signaling machinery remains functional but requires additional activation. The comparison to tachyzoite Ca2+ oscillations is supported by citation to Lovett and Sibley 2003.

result: Ca2+ chelator BAPTA-AM, PKG inhibitor compound 1, and CDPK1 inhibitor 3-MB-PP1 all significantly impaired gliding motility of both tachyzoites and bradyzoites, confirming a key role of Ca2+ signaling in parasite motility. Bradyzoites displayed shorter gliding distances compared to tachyzoites as measured by trail lengths. Despite having dampened Ca2+ stores and reduced responses to agonists when intracellular, extracellular bradyzoites require Ca2+ signaling to activate gliding motility.
evaluation: Claims C93-C95 are supported by gliding trail assays using stage-specific surface markers (Figure 7E-F). The use of three different inhibitors targeting different points in the Ca2+ signaling pathway (BAPTA-AM for Ca2+ chelation, compound 1 for PKG, 3-MB-PP1 for CDPK1) provides strong evidence for Ca2+ dependence. Statistical analyses confirm significant effects (Kruskal-Wallis with Dunn's correction, p<0.001, n=20 from 3 independent experiments). The conclusion (C95) is well-supported.

result: Bradyzoites substantially recovered stored Ca2+ when incubated with exogenous Ca2+ and glucose for 1 hr compared to 10 min, with more modest recovery in Ca2+ alone. Bradyzoites secreted more MIC2-GLuc after 1 hr treatment with Ca2+ and glucose. Bradyzoites substantially recovered all forms of gliding motility after 1 hr incubation with both Ca2+ and glucose, while very few bradyzoites could glide with Ca2+ or glucose alone.
evaluation: Claims C96-C99 are supported by Ca2+ imaging (Figure 8A-B), microneme secretion assays (Figure 8C), and motility assays (Figure 8D). The time course (10 min vs 1 hr) and factorial design (±Ca2+, ±glucose) provide strong evidence for synergistic effects. Statistical analyses confirm significant differences (Mann-Whitney test, p<0.01 for secretion; Kruskal-Wallis with Dunn's correction, p<0.01 for motility). The data demonstrate that both Ca2+ and glucose are required for optimal recovery.

result: Either glucose or glutamine significantly increased gliding motility by bradyzoites, indicating that either carbon source can be used to produce ATP for maintaining gliding motility. However, oligomycin A (ATP synthase inhibitor) blocked glucose-dependent gliding, indicating an essential role of mitochondrial electron transport chain in ATP production for supporting bradyzoite gliding motility.
evaluation: Claims C100 and C102 are supported by motility assays using different carbon sources and metabolic inhibitors (Figure 8E-F). The experimental design tests glucose vs glutamine (different entry points into metabolism) and uses 2-DOG (glycolysis inhibitor) and oligomycin A (oxidative phosphorylation inhibitor) to dissect metabolic requirements. Statistical analyses confirm significant effects (Kruskal-Wallis with Dunn's correction, p<0.05 or p<0.001). The finding that oligomycin A blocks glucose-dependent gliding indicates oxidative phosphorylation is essential, even when glucose is present.

result: HPLC-UV analysis showed that after 1 hr incubation in EC buffer with Ca2+ and glucose, bradyzoites had significantly higher ATP, ADP, and AMP levels, demonstrating enhanced ATP production. In contrast, tachyzoite ATP and ADP levels did not change significantly despite increased AMP. Bradyzoites displayed significantly increased ATP/ADP ratio and energy charge after 1 hr while tachyzoites showed no obvious changes. Collectively, exogenous Ca2+ and glucose activate bradyzoite gliding motility via restoration of ATP levels and Ca2+ stores.
evaluation: Claims C103-C106 are supported by HPLC-UV measurements of adenine nucleotides (Figure 8G-I, Figure 8—figure supplement 1A-C). The HPLC method provides quantitative measurements of ATP, ADP, and AMP levels. Standard curves were used for quantification. Data come from two independent biological replicates with three technical replicates each. Statistical analyses confirm significant differences (multiple Student's t-tests, p<0.05, p<0.01, or p<0.001). The calculation of ATP/ADP ratio and energy charge provides standard metrics for cellular energy status. The conclusion (C106) is well-supported by the combined data.

result: The study demonstrates that Ca2+ responses, microneme secretion, and egress by bradyzoites are highly attenuated compared to tachyzoites. Dampened Ca2+ responses were evident in in vitro cysts, naturally occurring cysts in muscle cells, and ex vivo tissue cysts from infected mice. Reduced responses were not simply due to the cyst environment as similar dampened signals were observed in extracellular bradyzoites. Ratiometric Ca2+ imaging revealed lower resting Ca2+ and reduced stored Ca2+ associated with downregulation of Ca2+-ATPases. When released and provided with Ca2+ and glucose, bradyzoites exhibited Ca2+-dependent gliding motility, demonstrating remarkable physiological flexibility.
evaluation: Claims C107-C110, C112, C114 represent the major conclusions of the study, synthesizing findings from multiple experimental systems (in vitro pH stress induction, spontaneous differentiation in C2C12 cells, ex vivo cysts from mice, extracellular bradyzoites). The conclusions are well-supported by extensive data from Figures 1-8 using multiple complementary approaches (egress assays, microneme secretion reporters, Ca2+ imaging with multiple indicators, ratiometric measurements, gene expression analysis, metabolic measurements). The demonstration of physiological flexibility (C114) is supported by the recovery experiments in Figure 8.

result: The dampened Ca2+ signaling responses of bradyzoites reflect adaptations well suited to the long-term intracellular lifestyle of these chronic stages. Reduced Ca2+ storage, dampened Ca2+ signaling, and lower energy state may reflect the sessile nature of the intracellular cyst, which prolongs chronic infection. The rapid metabolic recovery of otherwise quiescent bradyzoites may be important for maintaining chronic infection within a single host and ensuring robust cellular invasion upon transmission to the next host.
evaluation: Claims C113, C144, C150 represent interpretations of the biological significance of the findings. These interpretations are reasonable given the data showing: (1) dampened Ca2+ signaling and reduced energy in intracellular bradyzoites (Figures 1-6), (2) rapid recovery of Ca2+, ATP, and motility when provided with Ca2+ and glucose (Figure 8), and (3) the known biology of chronic T. gondii infection with periodic cyst rupture and reinvasion. The interpretations are appropriately framed as inferences rather than direct observations.

result: The study demonstrates that bradyzoites show minimal egress from in vitro-differentiated cysts and are refractory to stimulation of microneme secretion in response to Ca2+ agonists that normally trigger these responses in tachyzoites. Ca2+ signaling was significantly dampened in bradyzoites as reflected in delayed Ca2+ spikes and lower magnitude of cytosolic Ca2+ increases. Reduced Ca2+ responses were confirmed in naturally formed bradyzoites in C2C12 cells and ex vivo cysts from infected mice, and in extracellular bradyzoites, ruling out artifacts from alkaline pH stress or reduced cyst permeability. Ratiometric measurements confirmed lower resting Ca2+ levels and quantitatively decreased Ca2+ responses in bradyzoites.
evaluation: Claims C115-C121 summarize key findings from the Discussion section, which are well-supported by the experimental data presented in Results. The claims accurately reflect the data from Figures 1-6 and appropriately cite supporting literature (Frénal et al. 2017, Carruthers 2019). The use of multiple experimental systems (in vitro pH induction, C2C12 cells, ex vivo cysts, extracellular bradyzoites) and multiple reporters (GCaMP6f, Fluo-8 AM, ratiometric GCaMP6f/mTagBFP2) provides strong support for the conclusions.

result: Bradyzoites likely possess different mechanisms to control Ca2+ homeostasis, including differences in expression of Ca2+ channels and pumps relative to tachyzoites. Bradyzoites showed reduced responses to ionomycin and thapsigargin (ER Ca2+ release) and to NH4Cl (acidic store Ca2+ release). Consistent with these dampened responses, bradyzoites showed significantly reduced expression of Ca2+-ATPases TgSERCA and TgA1, as well as TgA2, Ca2+/H+ exchanger, and TRPPL-2. The reduced expression of Ca2+ channels and pumps would result in a general reduction of stored Ca2+.
evaluation: Claims C122-C127 represent mechanistic interpretations supported by the combined data from Ca2+ imaging experiments (Figure 5D-E) and gene expression analysis (Figure 6G). The interpretation (C122) is appropriately framed as likely/inference. The reduced responses to specific agonists (C123-C124) are directly supported by data. The reduced gene expression (C125-C126) is supported by RT-PCR data with appropriate citations. The conclusion linking reduced expression to reduced stored Ca2+ (C127) is a reasonable inference.

result: It is possible that reduced Ca2+ levels in bradyzoites reflect limitations on Ca2+ availability from the host cell, since prior studies showed tachyzoites acquire intracellular Ca2+ from this source. Reduced ER Ca2+ could impact mitochondrial Ca2+ since Ca2+ can be transferred directly from ER to mitochondria through membrane contact sites in mammalian cells, which is essential for oxidative phosphorylation and ATP production.
evaluation: Claims C128-C129 represent speculative hypotheses about mechanisms that were not directly tested in this study. While the speculation is reasonable and supported by citations to relevant literature (Vella et al. 2021 for C128; Cárdenas et al. 2010, Gherardi et al. 2020 for C129), these mechanisms were not experimentally validated in the current work. The claims are appropriately framed as possibilities/speculation. Additional experiments would be needed to test these hypotheses.

result: Bradyzoites are surrounded by a cyst wall comprising an outer compact layer and inner sponge-like layer enriched in dense granule proteins, glycoproteins like CST1, and carbohydrates. This architecture may create a barrier to egress since bradyzoites could activate motility but not efficiently emerge from intact cysts. Proteolytic release by trypsin did not result in immediate Ca2+ or motility changes, suggesting cyst wall degradation does not trigger egress-like processes. However, a subset of released bradyzoites spontaneously underwent gliding motility with Ca2+ oscillations similar to tachyzoites. When incubated with extracellular Ca2+, the percentage of motile bradyzoites increased dramatically.
evaluation: Claims C130-C135 integrate structural knowledge of the cyst wall (C130-C131, supported by citations to Lemgruber et al. 2011, Tu et al. 2019, Petri et al. 2001, Tomita et al. 2013, 2017) with experimental observations from the current study (C132-C135, supported by data in Figure 7). The interpretation that the cyst wall creates a barrier (C132) is reasonable given the data. The observations about trypsin release (C133) and subsequent motility (C134-C135) are directly supported by experimental data with appropriate citations (Lovett and Sibley 2003, Pace et al. 2014, Borges-Pereira et al. 2015).

result: Unlike tachyzoites which contain sufficient Ca2+ stores and energy to be independent of external carbon sources during the first hour after liberation, bradyzoites require an external carbon source to regain Ca2+ stores and ATP levels. Either glucose or glutamine was capable of synergizing with Ca2+ to restore bradyzoite motility, though inhibitor studies indicate oxidative phosphorylation is required to restore optimal energy levels. Bradyzoites have intrinsically low ATP/ADP ratios but recovered substantially when incubated extracellularly for 1 hr in Ca2+ and glucose. Collectively, bradyzoites are characterized by both low Ca2+ stores and low ATP levels, but respond to changes in the extracellular environment to restore both energy levels and Ca2+ signaling systems needed for motility.
evaluation: Claims C136-C140 are supported by the metabolic recovery experiments in Figure 8. The comparison to tachyzoites (C136) is supported by citation to Lin et al. 2011. The carbon source experiments (C137) are supported by data in Figure 8F with appropriate citations (Blume et al. 2009, MacRae et al. 2012). The requirement for oxidative phosphorylation (C138) is supported by oligomycin A inhibitor data. The ATP/ADP measurements (C139) are supported by HPLC data in Figure 8G-I. The overall conclusion (C140) is well-supported by the combined data.

result: During natural egress, bradyzoites may rely on endogenous energy stores such as amylopectin, especially since Ca2+ levels and CDPK2 influence storage and utilization of this carbohydrate. The mechanisms inducing cyst wall turnover in vivo are unclear, though host macrophages may contribute by secreting chitinase that can lyse cysts, and parasite hydrolases like GRA56 may be involved. In vitro studies suggest that once the cyst wall is ruptured, bradyzoites respond to higher levels of Ca2+ and glucose in the extracellular environment to regain motility. Emergence from tissue cysts that rupture in muscle or brain, or following oral ingestion, is likely to provide an environment to recharge bradyzoites.
evaluation: Claims C141, C145-C146, C148 represent speculative hypotheses about natural egress and cyst rupture mechanisms that were not directly tested in this study. While the speculation is reasonable and supported by citations to relevant literature (Uboldi et al. 2015 for C141; Nance et al. 2012 for C145; Nadipuram et al. 2020 for C146), these mechanisms were not experimentally validated in the current work. Claim C147 is better supported as it summarizes in vitro findings, though the extrapolation to in vivo conditions remains speculative. Additional in vivo experiments would be needed to test these hypotheses.

result: Previous in vitro studies have shown that motile bradyzoites released from ruptured cysts have the ability to reinvade new host cells, establishing new cysts without an intermediate growth stage as tachyzoites.
evaluation: Claim C149 is a statement about prior work, supported by citation to Dzierszinski et al. 2004. This provides relevant context for interpreting the current findings about bradyzoite motility recovery, though it was not directly tested in the current study.

result: Stimulation of Ca2+ signaling is important in breaking dormancy and pollen germination in plants, and in initiation of the cell cycle in animal cells.
evaluation: Claims C142-C143 provide comparative context from other biological systems, supported by appropriate citations (Pang et al. 2007, Steinhorst and Kudla 2013 for plants; Humeau et al. 2018 for animal cells). This contextualizes the role of Ca2+ signaling in reactivation across different organisms.
